adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue in the diff. Looking at lines 132-135 in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, when the enable API returns 200, it calls `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` instead of immediately calling `onEnable()`. The `onEnable()` is only called when the user clicks the 'Close' button (line 268-271). If the user dismisses the dialog by other means (clicking outside, pressing escape, browser navigation, etc.) after 2FA is successfully enabled on the server but before clicking Close, the parent component won't be notified via `onEnable()`, leaving the UI state inconsistent with the server state. The backup codes are generated during setup (line 89-97), not during enable, so they would have been shown, but the parent state would be stale.

TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` makes replacement codes impossible to generate while 2FA is enabled even though the new missing-code UI explicitly directs affected users to generate them in Settings.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real logical inconsistency. In setup.ts lines 41-43, there's a check `if (user.twoFactorEnabled) return res.status(400).json({ error: ErrorCode.TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled })` that prevents regenerating backup codes when 2FA is already enabled. However, the new UI in login.tsx shows a 'missing_backup_codes' error message that tells users 'Please generate them in your settings' (from common.json). This creates a contradiction: users who have 2FA enabled but no backup codes (or used all their codes) cannot generate new ones because the setup endpoint blocks them. This is a real functional bug in the new backup code feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:149 — `await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: user.id }` unconditionally replaces a stale decrypted list, so concurrent logins can both accept the same one-time code or can consume different codes and have the last writer resurrect the other code.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the backup code consumption logic. Looking at the diff in next-auth-options.ts lines 128-157, the code: 1) decrypts backup codes from the database, 2) checks if the supplied code exists in the array, 3) sets that index to null, 4) re-encrypts and updates the database. Between steps 1 and 4, another concurrent login could read the same backup codes list (before the update), validate the same backup code, and both would succeed. The last writer would overwrite the other's changes, potentially resurrecting a used code or losing the record of a consumed code. This is a classic read-modify-write race condition with no locking or atomic operation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:63 — `await prisma.user.update({` has no compare-and-set or transaction around the preceding enabled-state read, so concurrent setup requests both return success but every response except the last database writer contains backup codes and a TOTP secret that will not work.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the setup.ts endpoint. Looking at the diff, the code reads user state, generates backup codes and secret, then does a prisma.user.update without any transaction or optimistic locking. If two concurrent setup requests occur, both will generate different secrets/backup codes, but only the last write wins. The earlier responses will return backup codes and secrets that are immediately overwritten and won't work. This is a valid concurrency bug in the new backup codes feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/components/settings/EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx:278 — `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is neither awaited nor caught and the next line always shows a success toast, so clipboard denial or failure tells the user their recovery codes were copied even though nothing was written.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff at line 278 in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, the code is: `navigator.clipboard.writeText(backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode).join("\n"));` followed immediately by `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success");`. The clipboard API returns a Promise, but it's not awaited and there's no .catch() handler. The success toast is shown unconditionally on the next line regardless of whether the clipboard write succeeded or failed. This means if clipboard access is denied or fails for any reason, the user will still see a success message saying their codes were copied when they weren't. This is a real bug that could lead to users losing their backup codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/components/settings/EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx:135 — `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` records server success only in local step state while `onEnable()` is deferred to the custom Close button, so dismissing the dialog via Escape, its close control, or an interruption leaves the owner UI claiming 2FA is disabled after the server enabled it and can discard the only displayed codes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, when the TOTP code is verified successfully (response.status === 200), the code calls `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` instead of immediately calling `onEnable()`. The `onEnable()` callback is only called when the user clicks the 'Close' button in the DisplayBackupCodes step. If the user dismisses the dialog via Escape key, clicking outside, or the dialog's built-in close control, `onEnable()` is never called. This means the parent component's state won't be updated to reflect that 2FA is now enabled on the server, creating a UI inconsistency. Additionally, the backup codes displayed would be lost without being saved. This is a real correctness/UX bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:61 — `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes an unvalidated string, so a truthy JSON number or object throws a TypeError and produces a raw 500 instead of the 4xx backup-code error this malformed request requires.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows at line 61 in disable.ts: `const index = backupCodes.indexOf(req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""));`. The code only checks `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && req.body.backupCode)` which is a truthy check. If req.body.backupCode is a number or object (valid JSON), it would be truthy but calling .replaceAll() on it would throw a TypeError since replaceAll is a string method. This would result in an unhandled exception and a 500 error instead of a proper 400 error with ErrorCode.IncorrectBackupCode. This is a real input validation bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/components/settings/TwoFactorAuthAPI.ts:23 — `return fetch("/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable", {` supplies no timeout or abort signal, so a stalled request never reaches the modal's `finally`, leaving the disable action permanently loading and blocked until the component is destroyed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the fetch call in TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable() has no timeout or abort signal. Looking at the diff, the disable function is modified to accept a new backupCode parameter and the fetch call is shown. In DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx, the handleDisable function calls this API and has a finally block that sets isDisabling to false. If the fetch hangs indefinitely, the finally block would never execute, leaving the modal in a loading state. However, this is not a bug introduced by this diff - the lack of timeout existed before (the diff only adds the backupCode parameter). This is more of a pre-existing architectural concern that the reviewer noticed while reviewing related changes. It's a valid observation but not a defect introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx:49 — Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the shared `PasswordField` visibility button is unrelated to 2FA backup codes and removes that control from keyboard tab order everywhere `PasswordField` is used.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `tabIndex={-1}` being added to the PasswordField component in packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx. This is a shared UI component used across the application, not just for 2FA. The finding correctly identifies that this change removes the password visibility toggle button from keyboard tab order everywhere PasswordField is used, which is an accessibility concern. adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:121 — Because `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` skips password verification for any nonempty TOTP value while line 131 still accepts `credentials.backupCode`, an attacker can submit a dummy TOTP plus a stolen recovery code to create a session without the account password.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the code flow. Looking at the diff in next-auth-options.ts, the password verification happens BEFORE the 2FA check (lines 119-127 in the original flow). The condition `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` at line 121 is checking whether to verify the password, and password verification occurs regardless of backup code presence. The 2FA logic (starting around line 128) only runs AFTER password has been verified. The backup code path (line 128-149) and TOTP path are alternatives for the second factor, but both require the password to have been verified first. The finding incorrectly claims password verification is skipped when using backup codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:149 — The decrypted recovery-code list is checked and then replaced with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`, so concurrent requests can authenticate with the same one-time code or overwrite each other and resurrect an already-consumed code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in next-auth-options.ts lines 128-160, when a backup code is used: (1) backupCodes are decrypted, (2) the index is found, (3) backupCodes[index] is set to null, (4) prisma.user.update is called. There's no transaction or atomic operation - if two concurrent requests use the same backup code, both could pass the indexOf check before either completes the update, allowing the same one-time code to be used twice. This is a real race condition vulnerability in the authentication flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts:53 — `await expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts that the Promise object is truthy, so the test stays green when enabling 2FA leaves the switch unchecked.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a bug in the test code. Looking at line 48-49 in the diff, `page.locator(...).isChecked()` returns a Promise, and calling `.toBeTruthy()` on a Promise object will always pass because the Promise object itself is truthy. The diff even includes a FIXME comment at lines 47-48 acknowledging this exact issue: 'FIXME: this passes even when switch is not checked, compare to test below which checks for data-state="checked" and works as expected'. The correct approach shown later in the file (line 118) uses `await expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch][data-state="checked"]`)).toBeVisible()` which properly awaits and checks the actual state.
